requirement: Offshore turbine technicians will require a higher level of training to enter and perform work on an offshore turbine than technicians that are trained for land-based turbines.
The additional training should anticipate and cover specific differences between the offshore wind power plant's electrical design and the base training received by U.S. electrical workers.
On most issues, the substation group defaulted to American Petroleum Institute (API), ANSI, and IEEE standards for offshore wind substations.

API Recommended Practice 14F, "Design and Installation of Electrical Systems for Offshore Production Platforms" was frequently identified as an applicable U.S. standard because specific electrical safety requirements for electrical installations located offshore are covered.
Turbine designs comply with international codes and standards
Turbine models are type certified against the design basis, in accordance with IECRE OD 501

Evaluating the design basis relative to OSHA regulations, United States Coast Guard (USCG) regulations, and leading standards from IEEE, National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), and others to meet safety objectives
scope: Offshore wind turbines in the United States
source: SGRE's design process for the U.S. market

requirement: Evaluating the gaps between the global design basis and U.S. codes and standards on a case-by-case basis. If safety can be improved with reasonable effort, design modifications are made
scope: Offshore wind turbines in the United States
source: SGRE's design process for the U.S. market

requirement: IEEE 1584 and NFPA 70E are the most appropriate standards for the U.S. market
NFPA 70E and Canadian Standards Association (CSA) Z462 are essentially the same document (CSA is the Canadian standard and is harmonized with NFPA 70E)
scope: U.S. and Canadian offshore wind farms

requirement: Use of IEC standards should constitute compliance, and the arc flash label can be applied per IEEE 1584/NFPA 70E
scope: Offshore wind farms with experience in European markets

requirement: The developer shall establish a Safety Management System (SMS) that complies with 30 CFR 585 and is approved by BOEM/BSEE

Only U.S. lockout/tagout standards and practices should be followed. Project owners will not allow anyone who does not follow NFPA 70 E and OSHA standards for control of hazardous energies and lockout/tagout to work on a project site.

International standards include requirements for the design of equipment for lockout/tagout, which should be considered compatible with the process requirements from OSHA and NFPA 70E. These standards include IEC 60204-1 (e.g., Section 5.4) for electrical installations, as well as ISO 12100 (e.g., Section 6.2.11.1) for general machine safety and ISO 4413 (e.g., Section 5.4.7.2.1) for fluid power systems (hydraulics).
IEC 61400-22 be replaced with IECRE OD-501, 'BS' (British Standard) be removed from EN 61400-22, and BS PD IEC WT 01 be removed from the table. ISO 9001 be added to the table.
scope: Offshore wind turbine certification and testing
source: IEC 61400-22, IECRE OD-501, EN 61400-22, BS PD IEC WT 01, ISO 9001

requirement: IEC 61400-1 and IEC 61400-3-1 include commissioning testing requirements, whereas other standards include (such as IEC 60204-1) verification and testing requirements. CSA SPE-1000-13 is used for field evaluation of electrical equipment.
scope: Offshore wind turbine testing and commissioning

requirement: IEC standards for switchgear and associated equipment are preferred over U.S. and European standards regarding the need for visual confirmation of contact status (i.e., open or closed) for switchgear.

IEEE C37.122 standard does not appear to be fully implemented by any vendors of gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) above 52 kV. All available GIS at the high voltages required for an offshore substation are built and tested to IEC 62271.
scope: Offshore substations with GIS above 52 kV

requirement: Vendors can customize IEC's GIS to meet additional requirements of IEEE, but the Factory Acceptance Tests are performed according to IEC and the tests are different from IEEE.
Use of fully IEC-compliant local control cabinets or hybrid local control cabinet designs that are built to IEC standards, but also meet all of the practical requirements of IEEE C37.21.
If a hybrid IEC/IEEE local control cabinet is used, then type/colors of cables used will ensure a consistent design.
scope: Offshore substations with hybrid IEC/IEEE local control cabinets
